newsitem.title: USA: Consumer debt no threat to recovery -- Fed's Lindsey.
newsitem.headline: Consumer debt no threat to recovery -- Fed's Lindsey.

text.p: The steep rise in consumer debt does not pose a threat to the continued expansion of the U.S. economy or the soundness of U.S. banks, Federal Reserve Governor Lawrence Lindsey said Thursday.

"The (Fed) Board does not believe that current debt service levels are a necessary impediment to continued economic expansion," Lindsey said in prepared testimony to the House Banking Committee. "We also see no reason to believe that this expansion of consumer debt on the balance sheets of the nation's banks is any cause to worry about their underlying safety and soundness."
Lindsey said the Fed was carefully monitoring the effect higher debt levels were having on the economy.

Consumers can probably continue to maintain current spending patterns by increasing their debt further for the foreseeable future, he added. He noted that overall employment conditions are "quite good," and that consumer confidence is high.

"The Federal Reserve believes that the best policy is to continue to monitor and study developments in this area, but that no immediate regulatory or legislative action is warranted," he told the lawmakers.
Lindsey said banks are already growing more conservative in handing out consumer loans in recognition of rising credit delinquencies and personal bankruptcies.
But he said it would be "premature" to conclude that the pullback by banks on consumer loans will trigger a recession.
"We ... do not believe that the reduced willingness to extend credit at the current time is sufficiently widespread to create any significant macroeconomic risk to the expansion," he said.
He also played down concerns that excessive debt service burdens among consumers could pose a risk to the expansion.
"While high, the current level of debt service payments is not out of the range of past experience," Lindsey said.
Besides, the balance sheet of the household sector as a whole has improved substantially in recent years, in part because of the dramatic increase in the stock market, he said.
"From an economic point of view, there is nothing wrong with consumers increasing their debt, per se," he added.

Much of the recent increase in household debt has occured in middle and upper middle income families. Lindsey suggested they may be taking on added debt because of expectations their wages will pick up after lagging in recent years.
